#### **Aim :**
To construct Chi-square control chart and also plot the control contour.

#### **Problem :**
When we are monitoring a process with $p=2$ continuously for **temperature and pressure**. Then the process has establish the known population parameter, i.e. **mean vector**
$$
\mu =
\begin{bmatrix}
\mu_1 \\
\mu_2
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
50 \\
100
\end{bmatrix}
$$
and **variance-covariance matrix** is 
$$
\Sigma =
\begin{bmatrix}
10 & 20 \\
20 & 50
\end{bmatrix}
$$
If the sample vector are :
$$
X_1 =
\begin{bmatrix}
54 \\
108
\end{bmatrix}, \qquad
X_2 =
\begin{bmatrix}
54 \\
92
\end{bmatrix}
$$

then construct the **chi-square control chart** with $2-d.f.$

In both cases draw the control plot for chi-square Control Limits or calculated Control Limits with respect to tabulated Control Limits

#### **Theory :**

##### **<u>Chi-Square Control Chart</u>**
A **chi-square control chart** is a statistical process control technique used to monitor a **multivariate process**, where two or more quality characteristics are measured simultaneously.

When the process mean vector and covariance matrix are known, the chi-square statistic is used to determine whether an observation is consistent with the normal operating condition of the process.

- ##### **Mahalanobis Distance**
  For an observation vector $X$, with known mean vector $\mu$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$, the squared Mahalanobis distance is
$$
\chi^2 = (X-\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(X-\mu)
$$

  If the observations follow a multivariate normal distribution,
$$
X \sim N_p(\mu,\Sigma)
$$

  then
$$
\chi^2 \sim \chi^2_p
$$

  where $p$ is the number of quality characteristics.

- ##### **Control Limits**
  For the chi-square control chart, the control limits are:
  Center Line :
$$
CL = p
$$

  Lower Control Limit :
$$
LCL = 0
$$
  
  Upper Control Limit :
$$
UCL = \chi^2_{p,1-\alpha}
$$

  where:

  - $p$ = number of variables
  - $\alpha$ = significance level
  - $\chi^2_{p,1-\alpha}$ = $1-\alpha$ quantile
  of the chi-square distribution with $p$ degrees
  of freedom.
  
- ##### **Decision Rule**
  For each sample, calculate
$$
\chi_i^2=(X_i-\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(X_i-\mu)
$$

  The decision rule is:
    
  - If $\chi_i^2 \leq UCL$, the process is **in
  control**.
  - If $\chi_i^2 > UCL$, the process is **out of
  control**.

  The LCL is zero because the squared Mahalanobis
  distance cannot be negative.

- ##### **Control Contour**
  The chi-square control chart can also be represented graphically by a **control contour**.

  The control contour is given by
$$
(X-\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(X-\mu)
=
\chi^2_{p,1-\alpha}
$$

  For two variables ($p=2$), this equation forms/represents an **ellipse** centered at the process mean $\mu$.

  - Points **inside the ellipse** indicate an **in-control** process.
  - Points **outside the ellipse** indicate an **out-of-control** process.


#### **Code and Calculation :**
Here 

 - $X_1$ : represents the **Temperature**
 - $X_2$ : represents the **Pressure**
```{r}
# -: Chi-square control chart :-

# Given
alpha <- 0.0027
p <- 2

# Control limits
CL  <- p
LCL <- 0
UCL <- qchisq(1 - alpha, df = p)

cat("The Center Line (CL) is :", CL)
cat("The Lower Control Limit (LCL) is :", LCL)
cat("The Upper Control Limit (UCL) is :", UCL)

# Known population mean
mu <- c(50, 100)

# Given covariance matrix
Sigma <- matrix(c(10, 20,
              20, 50), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)

# Inverse of covariance matrix
Sigma_inv <- solve(Sigma)

# Observations
X <- rbind(
  X1 = c(54, 108),
  X2 = c(54, 92)
)

# Calculate chi-square statistics
chisq.stat <- apply(X, 1, function(x) {
  d <- x - mu
  t(d) %*% Sigma_inv %*% d
})

chisq.stat <- as.numeric(chisq.stat)

# Display results
results <- data.frame(
  Observation = rownames(X),
  Chi_square = chisq.stat,
  Status = ifelse(chisq.stat > UCL,
                  "Out of control",
                  "In control")
)

print(results)

# -: Manually Ploting chi-square control chart :-
plot(1:2, chisq.stat,
     type = "b",
     pch = 19,
     xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Sample",
     ylab = expression(chi^2),
     main = expression(paste(chi^2, "Control Chart")),
     ylim = c(0, 30),
     xlim = c(0.8, 2.7))

# X-axis labels
axis(1, at = 1:2, labels = c("X1", "X2"))

# Control lines
abline(h = UCL, lty = 2, lwd = 2)
abline(h = CL,  lty = 3, lwd = 2)
abline(h = LCL, lty = 2, lwd = 2)

# Control limit labels
text(2.1, UCL, paste0("UCL = ", round(UCL, 3)), pos = 4)
text(2.1, CL,  paste0("CL = ", CL), pos = 4)
text(2.1, LCL, paste0("LCL = ", LCL), pos = 4)

# Highlight out-of-control point
points(which(chisq.stat > UCL),
       chisq.stat[chisq.stat > UCL],
       pch = 19)

# Legend
legend("topleft",
       legend = c("Statistic", "UCL", "CL", "LCL"),
       lty = c(1, 2, 3, 2),
       pch = c(19, NA, NA, NA),
       bty = "n")

# -: Ploting chi-square control chart using QCC package :-
# Installing the required libraries
# install.packages("qcc")
library(qcc)

qcc.chisq <- qcc(
  chisq.stat,
  type = "xbar.one",
  center = CL,
  limits = c(LCL, UCL),
  labels = rownames(X),
  title = expression(Chi-square ~ "Control Chart using in-built package QCC"),
  xlab = "Sample",
  ylab = expression(chi^2)
)
```

```{r}
# -: Chi-square contour plot :-

# Installing the required libraries
# install.packages("ellipse")
library(ellipse)

# Critical chi-square value
crit <- qchisq(1 - alpha, df = 2)

# Generating control ellipse
ell <- ellipse(
  x = Sigma,
  centre = mu,
  level = 1 - alpha,
  npoints = 500
)

# Ploting
plot(ell,
     type = "l",
     lwd = 2,
     asp = 1,
     xlab = expression(mu[1]),
     ylab = expression(mu[2]),
     main = expression(paste(
       chi^2, " Control Contour"
     )))

# Adding process mean
points(mu[1], mu[2],
       pch = 4,
       cex = 1.5,
       lwd = 2)

# Adding observations
points(X[,1], X[,2],
       pch = 19)

text(X[,1], X[,2],
     labels = rownames(X),
     pos = 4)

legend("topright",
       legend = c("Control contour",
                  "Process mean",
                  "Observations"),
       lty = c(1, NA, NA),
       pch = c(NA, 4, 19),
       bty = "n")
```

#### **Results :**
The $\chi^2$ control chart was constructed for $p=2$ variables at a significance level of $\alpha=0.0027$.

The calculated control limits are:
$$
CL=p=2
$$

$$
LCL=0
$$

$$
UCL=\chi^2_{2,0.9973}=11.82901
$$

The calculated $\chi^2$ values and their status are:

| Observation | Temprature | Pressure | $\chi^2$ value | Status |
|:-----------:|:-----------:|:-----------:|:-----------:|:-----------:|
| $X_1$ | 54 | 108 | 1.6 | In control |
| $X_2$ | 54 | 92 | 27.2 | Out of control |

From the $\chi^2$ control chart, $X_1$ lies below the upper control limit, whereas $X_2$ lies above the upper control limit.

Therefore, the first observation $X_1$ with **Temperature = 54 and Pressure = 108**, is **within the control limits** and hence represents an **in-control** condition because
$$
1.6 < 11.82901.
$$

However, the second observation $X_2$ with **Temperature = 54 and Pressure = 92**, is **outside the control limits** and hence represents an **out of control** condition because
$$
27.2 > 11.82901.
$$

The $\chi^2$ control contour is an ellipse centered at the process mean
$$
\mu=(50,100).
$$

Here, the $\chi^2$ control contour gives the same conclusion: $X_1$ lies **inside the control contour**, whereas $X_2$ lies **outside the control contour**.

#### **Conclusions :**
Thus, the multivariate process is **not completely in control**, because the second observation indicates an abnormal change in the combined **temperature-pressure** process. Since temperature remains at 54 for both observations, the major change between the two observations is the **pressure**, which decreases from 108 to 92 and make the process **out of control**.
